To challenge this, I will test a weighted combination using the same top-5 pool (pool4) but with inverse_error weights to see if giving more power to the historically best performers (NaiveMovingAverage, ARIMA) improves over simple agreement. This tests the "ranking stability" characteristic by leveraging the small pool where rankings are more consistent.

The current leader (dba on pool4) relies on a robust central-tendency measure over a small, high-performing subset. Since rankings are unstable (ranking_tau=-0.279) and seasonality is strong (seasonal_strength=0.6866), a weighted combination that leverages the specific strengths of models in different correlation groups (e.g., NaiveMovingAverage for recent trend vs. ARIMA/ETS for structure) might outperform simple pooling. I will test an inverse-error weighted combination on pool4, which is more granular than DBA but focused on the same high-quality subset.

The current leader (dba on pool4) relies on a robust geometric mean to handle unstable rankings in this seasonal regime. To test if a simpler, broader aggregation of the top performers yields better results without the complexity of DBA's geometric handling, I will try a plain arithmetic mean over the same high-performing pool (pool4). This tests the sensitivity of the combination method given the strong seasonality and model correlation.

The leader (dba pool=pool4) is only marginally better than other robust combinations on pool4, and the gap is indistinguishable. To break the tie, I will test a different combination method (softmax weighted mean) on the same high-performing model subset (pool4), which avoids the redundancy of simple mean/trimmed_mean already tested on this pool.

The current leader (dba pool=pool4) has a narrow margin over similar strategies on the same pool, suggesting the benefit comes from the specific model selection rather than the combination method itself. To test if a different pool composition helps, I will try a broad weighted average using `inverse_error` weights across the full pool to see if including more diverse models (or correcting for their errors) improves robustness against the unstable ranking.

The leader (dba pool4) exploits the strong seasonality by focusing on the top 5 models that handle the cycle well. To test if a more robust, less peaky combination can beat DBA's sensitivity to the specific top-5 selection, I will evaluate a weighted mean of the entire pool using inverse error weights, which should downweight the noisy outliers in the full pool while retaining diversity.

The current leader (dba on pool4) performs well, but the untried 'median' on pool4 offers a robust alternative to DBA by being less sensitive to extreme outliers within the top-5 group, which may help if the "seasonal_dominated" regime has periodic spikes.

Baseline equal-weighted mean to compare against trimmed_mean given ranking instability.

I will test Dynamic Bayes Averaging (dba), which adapts weights based on recent performance, to see if it can better handle the unstable ranking environment than a static equal-weighted mean.

The DBA leader exploits strong seasonality via dynamic alignment, but rankings are unstable (ranking_tau=-0.279). I will test a weighted combination using inverse error weights to leverage the top performers (NaiveMovingAverage, ARIMA) while reducing the noise from weaker models.

The series has strong seasonality and unstable model rankings, suggesting that simple robust aggregations like DBA or trimmed mean are good baselines, but weighted combinations of diverse models can outperform them. The current leader uses inverse error on a small pool (pool4). A different strategy is to use the full pool with a weighting scheme that accounts for recent performance trends rather than just static error, as rankings shift across windows. I will test `weights_error_trend` on the full pool to see if adapting to the most recent window's performance improves robustness.

A median combination is a robust alternative that mitigates the risk of any single model's outlier error, especially given the "unstable" ranking verdict and correlated error groups. I will test the median of the full pool to see if it provides better generalization than the weighted approach on this small validation set.
